puzzles.title: Tigers & Sheep
puzzles.tagline: 100 hungry, flawless logicians and one very nervous sheep.
puzzles.prompt:
On an island live 100 tigers and 1 sheep. Any tiger may eat the sheep — but the moment a tiger eats it, that tiger turns into a sheep, and can then be eaten by another tiger.

Every tiger is perfectly logical and, above all else, wants to stay alive. No tiger will make a move that gets itself eaten.

With 100 tigers, does the sheep get eaten, or is it safe?
rules: Any tiger may eat the sheep — but eating it turns the eater into a sheep.
A newly-made sheep can then be eaten by any remaining tiger.
Every tiger is perfectly logical and reasons flawlessly.
Above all, each tiger wants to survive; it never makes a move that leaves it exposed to being eaten.
hints: What happens with just 1 tiger? Then try 2. What changed?
When a tiger decides whether to eat, what does it need to be true about the world it wakes up in afterwards?
After a tiger eats, how many tigers are left facing the new sheep?
Line up the cases from small to large. What splits the safe outcomes from the eaten ones?
puzzles.whyExplanation:
Think about it from the smallest case up.

With 1 tiger, there is nothing to fear: that tiger eats the sheep and stays safe, because no other tiger is left to eat it. So 1 tiger → the sheep is eaten.

With 2 tigers, each tiger thinks: "If I eat the sheep, I become a sheep — and then the other tiger is exactly in the 1-tiger situation, where eating is safe. It would eat me." So neither dares. 2 tigers → the sheep is safe.

With 3 tigers, a tiger reasons: "If I eat, I become the sheep in a 2-tiger world — and we just saw the sheep is safe there. So I would survive." One of them eats. 3 tigers → eaten.

The pattern chains all the way up: a tiger eats only if, after it becomes the sheep, the remaining tigers form a "sheep is safe" situation. That flips with every added tiger. So the sheep is eaten when the number of tigers is ODD, and safe when it is EVEN.

100 is even — so the sheep is safe. All 100 tigers, each perfectly logical, hold back, because each knows that eating would only hand itself to the next tiger in line.

puzzles.title: Make the Target
puzzles.tagline: Pick the right tiles to land exactly on the number.
puzzles.prompt: You have a handful of number tiles. Add some of them together so the total lands exactly on the target. Each tile can be used at most once.
rules: Tap a tile to move it in or out of the tray.
The running total updates as you go — reach the target exactly.
hints: Which single tile gets you closest to 17 without going over?
If you start from the largest tile, how much is left to make up?
puzzles.whyExplanation: Reaching an exact total is a small taste of the "subset sum" problem: from a set of numbers, find a group that adds to a goal. Here, 3 + 5 + 9 = 17. With only a few tiles you can reason it out by hand; with hundreds, it becomes one of computer science's famously hard problems.

puzzles.title: Will It Balance?
puzzles.tagline: Slide the weight to find the balance point.
puzzles.prompt: A weight sits on the left of a balance beam. Slide the weight on the right until the beam settles level.
rules: Drag the right-hand weight along the beam to change its distance.
The beam tips according to real weight and distance — feel your way to level.
hints: What makes one side dip — is it the weight, the distance, or both together?
The left side is heavier but closer in. How could a lighter weight match it?
puzzles.whyExplanation: A beam balances when the turning effect (torque) is equal on both sides, and torque = weight x distance from the pivot. The left gives 4 x 3 = 12, so the lighter right weight of 3 must sit at distance 4 (3 x 4 = 12). A smaller weight can balance a larger one simply by sitting farther out.
